**Cause of the change in inventories not expected to be sold within one year.** These are reported as noncurrent inventories in Other noncurrent assets. They fell from $4,568 million at the end of 2023 to $2,663 million at the end of 2024. Note 8A says the decrease is primarily driven by a reduction in acquired Seagen inventory, including the acquisition-accounting fair value step-up. It adds that, based on current estimates and assumptions, there are no recoverability issues for these amounts.

The 10-K does not say whether that noncurrent inventory change affected operating cash flow as a source or a use of cash. It lists the change among the offsetting items.

NVIDIA's fiscal 2025 Form 10-K names two factors that affected gross margin in fiscal 2025. It does not give a fuller breakdown than these two.

**Favorable: higher Data Center revenue mix.** The 10-K says gross margin rose to 75.0% from 72.7% "primarily driven by a higher mix of Data Center revenue." Data Center revenue grew 142% year over year. The growth came mainly from demand for the Hopper architecture platform, which is used for large language models, recommendation engines and generative AI. NVIDIA also began shipping production Blackwell systems in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025.

**Unfavorable: inventory provisions, net of releases.**
- Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled $3.7 billion in fiscal 2025, up from $2.2 billion in fiscal 2024.
- Sales of previously reserved inventory and settlements of excess purchase obligations produced a provision release of $689 million in fiscal 2025, versus $540 million in fiscal 2024.
- The net effect lowered gross margin by 2.3% in fiscal 2025, compared with 2.7% in fiscal 2024. The smaller drag in fiscal 2025 meant a slightly smaller headwind than the prior year.

The 10-K also lists the items that make up cost of revenue, which are the cost categories that can move gross margin:
- semiconductor costs, including wafer fabrication, assembly, testing and packaging
- board and device costs
- manufacturing support costs
- final test yield fallout
- inventory and warranty provisions
- memory and component costs
- tariffs
- shipping costs
- acquisition-related intangible amortization
- license, development and service arrangement costs
- IP-related costs
- stock-based compensation for manufacturing personnel

The filing does not say how any of these items, apart from the inventory provisions, changed in fiscal 2025 or what they did to margin.

The relevant sections are pages 38 and 42 of the filing.

The filing gives two connected reasons, both on page K-43 of the MD&A.

1. **Rates include income taxes.** The filing says the rates BHE's regulated businesses charge customers "are largely based on the costs of business operations, including income taxes and a return on capital, and are subject to regulatory approval." Income taxes are therefore a cost that regulators build into customer rates, so BHE's results are better read after tax. If regulators don't allow certain costs in approved rates, operating results are adversely affected.

2. **After-tax earnings reflect how BHE is managed.** The filing says the discussion of BHE's operating results "is based on after-tax earnings, reflecting how the energy businesses are managed and evaluated."

The filing doesn't state this as a reason. A footnote does show that BHE's income tax line is a net benefit, not an expense. The benefit was $1.87 billion in 2024, and the effective tax rate was negative 81.6%. The footnote says the benefit "includes significant production tax credits primarily from wind-powered electricity generation." Those credits turned 2024 pre-tax earnings of $2.29 billion into after-tax earnings of $4.16 billion, so pre-tax figures would give a different picture of BHE's performance.

Boeing's 10-K gives two causes that it ties directly to lower 2024 commercial deliveries. Deliveries were 348 in 2024 and 528 in 2023.

1. **The IAM 751 strike.** The strike ran from September 13 to November 4, 2024. It paused production of the 737, 767, 777 and 777X, and production resumed in December. The filing says the work stoppage "significantly reduced aircraft deliveries in the second half of 2024" (MD&A Overview, p. 24).

2. **787 business-class seat delays.** The filing says "Delays associated with business class seats adversely impacted 2024 deliveries and will continue to impact deliveries in 2025" (787 Program, p. 37).

Several other causes are not clearly tied to deliveries:

- **737-9 grounding and slowed 737 production.** After the January 2024 Alaska Airlines accident, the FAA grounded the 737-9 and capped 737 production rate increases. The filing links these to production, costs and cash flow. It does not say they caused fewer deliveries.
- **Supply-chain constraints and the slower 787 rate.** The filing describes these as production-rate issues.
- **Delayed 737-7/-10 certification and 777X delays.** The filing discusses these as inventory, cost and reach-forward loss issues. It does not say they reduced 2024 deliveries.

The filing's revenue discussion cites "lower deliveries across all programs" alongside the 737-9 customer considerations, but it does not give a cause for the delivery decline there.

Boeing's 2025 Form 10-K gives few purposes or anticipated benefits for the Spirit AeroSystems acquisition. It states them briefly and doesn't develop them.

**Stated purpose (Note 2, Spirit Acquisition):** The acquisition "enables Boeing and Spirit to align our commercial production systems, including our Safety and Quality Management Systems, and our workforces to the same priorities, incentives and outcomes."

**Anticipated benefits (Risk Factors):** The filing names two expected benefits. These are "anticipated synergies" and "safety and quality improvements." It cites them in a warning that difficulties integrating Spirit could mean Boeing fails to realize them "in the expected timeframe or at all." It does not quantify the synergies. It also says integration could bring operational challenges, unforeseen expenses and a diversion of management attention.

**Related context in the filing:**
- **What Boeing acquired:** Spirit's Boeing-related commercial operations. These include fuselages for the 737, P-8 and KC-46 Tanker programs and major structures for the 767, 777 and 787 programs. The deal also covers Spirit's defense and aftermarket businesses, portions of its Belfast operations, and about 15,000 employees.
- **Earlier funding:** Boeing says it has funded Spirit with loans and advance payments since 2023. That funding supported Spirit's liquidity, production rate readiness, and 787 tooling and capital expenditures.
- **Link to the 737 quality problems:** Boeing's regulatory discussion says the FAA increased oversight of Spirit's quality and safety systems after the January 2024 737-9 door-plug accident. The filing doesn't say this is a reason for the deal.

The filing does not describe cost savings, margin improvement or strategic goals beyond the points above.

The fiscal 2024 Form 10-K gives these causes for the 217% Data Center growth (revenue of $47.5 billion):

**What drove demand for Data Center products**
- **Applications and industries (MD&A Fiscal Year 2024 Summary, p. 36):** The filing says "strong demand was driven by enterprise software and consumer internet applications, and multiple industry verticals including automotive, financial services, and healthcare."
- **Generative AI (MD&A overview, p. 34):** It says generative AI models "have driven increased demand for Data Center," while noting the long-term trajectory is unknown.
- **Hopper compute workloads (segment discussion, p. 39):** Compute demand centered on training and inference of large language models (LLMs), recommendation engines, and generative AI applications. The filing says demand for data center systems and products "surged" in fiscal 2024.

**What drove the growth of parts of Data Center revenue**
- **Compute (up 244%):** The filing attributes this to higher shipments of the NVIDIA Hopper GPU computing platform, used for the workloads above. The segment discussion (p. 39) gives the compute growth figure as 266%. The 266% appears to be a different measure from the 244% in the summary, and the filing doesn't explain the gap.
- **Networking (up 133%):** The filing attributes this to higher shipments of InfiniBand.

**Related context the filing describes (p. 36)**
- **AI inference products:** The filing says it launched AI inference platforms and introduced DGX Cloud and AI Foundations. It does not explicitly tie these to the revenue increase.
- **Inference share of revenue:** It estimates that about 40% of Data Center revenue in fiscal 2024 was for AI inference.

The filing also says Compute & Networking segment growth, up 215%, was due to higher Data Center revenue. It attributes the increase in U.S. revenue to higher U.S.-based Compute & Networking demand.

ExxonMobil's 2022 Form 10-K gives these causes for the decline in industry chemical margins:

- **Bottom-of-cycle conditions in Asia Pacific.** The 10-K describes the margin decline as "reflecting bottom-of-cycle conditions in Asia Pacific."
- **Increased industry capacity.** The 10-K cites "increased industry capacity" and, in the earnings factor analysis, "increased supply." It also lists "capacity additions" as a reason margins fell below the bottom of the 10-year range late in 2022.
- **Closure of the regional pricing disconnect between Asia and the Atlantic Basin.** The earnings factor analysis describes this as "normalization of regional prices during the year."
- **Weakening global demand.** The business environment discussion says margins fell below the bottom of the 10-year range late in 2022 "reflecting weakening global demand and capacity additions."

The filing gives the following causes for the fiscal 2023 declines in gross profit rate. I left out the factor it says partially offset the Walmart U.S. decline, which is price management driven by cost inflation.

**Consolidated (down 98 basis points)**
- Markdowns and merchandise mix in the U.S.
- Higher supply chain costs in Sam's Club.
- Inflation-related LIFO charges in Sam's Club.

**Walmart U.S. (down 85 basis points)**
- Net markdowns.
- Product mix shifts into lower-margin categories.
- Increased supply chain costs.

**Walmart International (down 50 basis points)**
- Continued growth in lower-margin formats and channels in China.
- Category mix shifts into lower-margin categories.

**Sam's Club (down 155 basis points)**
- Inventory write-downs.
- Elevated supply chain costs.
- Elevated eCommerce fulfillment costs.
- Inflation-related LIFO charges.

**Combined causes**
- Markdowns, including inventory write-downs.
- Unfavorable merchandise, category, format and channel mix, meaning shifts toward lower-margin categories, formats and channels.
- Higher supply chain costs, plus higher eCommerce fulfillment costs at Sam's Club.
- Inflation-related LIFO charges at Sam's Club.

These explanations come from the Results of Operations section of MD&A (pages 40–43).

The filing gives these drivers of fiscal 2026 growth in membership and other income. I left out the items it says partially offset the growth, such as lower recycling income.

**Company-wide (total up $0.3 billion, to $6.75 billion)**
- Growth in membership fee revenue globally.

**Walmart U.S. (up slightly, from $2,594 million to $2,624 million)**
- Double-digit growth in membership fee revenue from Walmart+.

**Sam's Club U.S. (up 8.7%, from $2,323 million to $2,525 million)**
- Growth in the membership base.
- Higher Plus penetration.
- Additional breakage income from unredeemed Sam's Cash rewards.

**Walmart International**
- The filing gives no separate explanation for the segment's membership and other income. It rose from $1,478 million to $1,565 million. The company-wide point about global membership fee growth is the only related driver.

In short, the filing attributes the growth to membership fee revenue growth (Walmart+ globally and in the U.S., and a larger and higher-tier Sam's Club membership base), plus extra Sam's Cash breakage income at Sam's Club.

ExxonMobil's 2023 Form 10-K gives these causes. The first set comes from the Upstream earnings discussion. The second set comes from the "Recent Business Environment" section.

**Upstream earnings discussion (p. 51)**
- Lower realizations cut Upstream earnings by $14,290 million. The filing attributes this to "lower gas prices and crude price moderation with growing liquids supply to address record demand."
- Unfavorable mark-to-market impacts of $2,380 million are included in that price effect.

**"Recent Business Environment" discussion (p. 49)**
- **Crude oil, first half of 2023:** Prices fell toward the average of the pre-COVID 10-year range (2010–2019). The filing says this was "impacted by higher inventory levels."
- **Crude oil, second half of 2023:** Prices rose modestly because of strong demand and OPEC+ actions to limit supply.
- **Natural gas, first nine months of 2023:** Prices fell significantly. Storage levels in the U.S. and Europe rose above historical averages because of higher supply and lower demand.
- **Natural gas, fourth quarter of 2023:** Prices improved on higher U.S. heating demand and supply interruptions in Europe and Asia. This brought them back above the 10-year range.
- **Broader context:** Energy markets began to normalize in 2023 from their 2022 highs. Those highs had followed industry underinvestment and supply tightness.

The 2023 Form 10-K gives these causes for the $2.6 billion rise in consumer net charge-offs:

- **Card Services normalization (the main cause).** The 10-K says the increase was "predominantly driven by Card Services, as the portfolio continued to normalize to pre-pandemic levels." Card Services net charge-offs rose from $2.4 billion to $4.7 billion.
- **Rising credit card delinquencies.** The 10-K says net charge-offs increased "as delinquencies have normalized." The 30+ day delinquency rate rose from 1.45% to 2.14%, and the 90+ day rate rose from 0.68% to 1.05%.
- **Growth in credit card loans.** The 10-K cites growth from new accounts and revolving balances, which "continued to normalize to pre-pandemic levels."
- **Higher scored auto charge-offs.** The 10-K attributes these to "the decline in used vehicle valuations." Auto net charge-offs rose from $144 million to $357 million.
- **Lower net recoveries on residential real estate (Home Lending).** The 10-K says net recoveries were lower "driven by lower prepayments due to higher interest rates." Home Lending net recoveries fell from $229 million to $56 million.

The filing gives one cause for the growth and one factor that weighed on the business.

**Cause of the growth.** In the Selected Product Discussion, Pfizer says growth was "primarily driven by continued strong uptake of the ATTR-CM indication in the U.S., developed Europe and Japan." The growth was strong in both regions:
- U.S. revenue rose 48%, from $613 million to $909 million.
- International revenue rose 64% (61% operationally), from $675 million to $1,106 million.

**Factor that weighed on the business.** In the COVID-19 section, the filing says Vyndaqel/Vyndamax "continued to see postponement of elective and diagnostic procedures in 2021 due to COVID-19." Pfizer adds that this effect "may subside in 2022 as COVID-19 vaccination and booster rates continue to increase and/or if COVID-19 cases subside."

Elsewhere, the filing lists Vyndaqel/Vyndamax among the products that contributed to Pfizer's overall operational revenue growth in 2021.

Five of the eight filings state a dollar amount for leases signed but not yet commenced. Pfizer, Berkshire Hathaway and Walmart do not.

| Company | Fiscal year-end | Not-yet-commenced leases, as stated (millions of dollars) |
|---|---|---|
| NVIDIA | Jan 29, 2023 | $463. These are operating leases, mainly for data centers, expected to start in fiscal 2024–2025 with terms of 2 to 8 years. |
| Apple | Sep 30, 2023 | $544. This is the future payments under additional leases, mainly for corporate facilities and retail space. They start between 2024 and 2026 with terms of 1 to 21 years. The filing gives no operating/finance split. |
| JPMorgan Chase | Dec 31, 2023 | $420. These are operating lease commitments, signed but not yet started. They begin between 2024 and 2026 with terms up to 21 years. |
| ExxonMobil | Dec 31, 2023 | Operating leases: $4,063. Finance leases: $2,256. Both are undiscounted commitments for leases not yet commenced. |
| Boeing | Dec 31, 2023 | $430. These are leases not yet commenced, mainly for a military-aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul hangar. They start in 2024 with terms of 2 to 27 years. |
| Pfizer | Dec 31, 2023 | None stated. The lease note gives only the maturity schedule for existing operating leases. |
| Berkshire Hathaway | Dec 31, 2023 | None stated. The lease note gives only existing operating lease payments. |
| Walmart | Jan 31, 2023 | None stated. The lease note gives only the maturity table for existing operating and finance leases. |

I read the lease notes directly for NVIDIA, Apple, ExxonMobil, Boeing, Pfizer, Berkshire and Walmart. For JPMorgan I read the lease note (Note 18). For Pfizer, Berkshire and Walmart I read only the lease notes and did not search the rest of the filings for a not-yet-commenced figure.

I left out Berkshire's $11,988 million of future operating lease receipts, because that is equipment it leases out to others, not leases it has signed as lessee.

Four of the eight filings report a completed acquisition of an entire named company in the fiscal year:

| Filing | Company acquired | Basis in the filing |
|---|---|---|
| Walmart, fiscal 2025 (year ended Jan 31, 2025) | VIZIO Holding Corp. | The Walmart U.S. segment completed the acquisition in December 2024 for net cash consideration of $1.9 billion. It added $1.375 billion of goodwill. |
| Berkshire Hathaway, 2025 | Bell Laboratories, LLC | Berkshire acquired it on July 31, 2025. The filing describes it as a maker of rodenticides and other rodent-control products. |
| Pfizer, 2025 | Metsera | Pfizer acquired the company on November 13, 2025, for $65.60 per share in cash plus contingent value rights. Total consideration was about $8.0 billion. |
| Boeing, 2025 | Spirit AeroSystems | Boeing completed the acquisition on December 8, 2025, through a share exchange. |

The other four filings do not qualify:

- **NVIDIA, fiscal 2025:** The filing mentions shares issued to key employees of "a company we acquired" but never names the company. Note 2 covers only the terminated Arm deal.
- **Apple, fiscal 2025:** I found no completed acquisition of a named company. I read this from the filing's structure and summaries rather than a full-text search.
- **JPMorgan Chase, 2025:** The only 2025 items are the settlement with the FDIC over the 2023 First Republic purchase price and the gain recorded on it. The acquisition itself closed in 2023.
- **ExxonMobil, 2025:** It acquired technology and assets from Superior Graphite, which is a purchase of assets rather than a whole company. Pioneer was acquired in 2024.

Berkshire's OxyChem purchase closed on January 2, 2026, after its year-end, so it is excluded. It was also a business acquired from Occidental rather than a company.

Three of the eight filings state a year-end supplier finance balance. I found no such disclosure in the other five, but I read only the relevant notes and sections, not every page.

| Company | Year-end balance (millions) | Where it appears |
|---|---|---|
| Walmart (Jan 31, 2025) | $5,725 | Note 1, "Supplier Financing Program Obligations": confirmed obligations outstanding at end of year |
| Boeing (Dec 31, 2025) | $1,994 | Note 15, "Supply Chain Financing Programs": ending balance of accounts payable to participating suppliers |
| Pfizer (Dec 31, 2025) | $574 | Note 8C, "Supplier Finance Program Obligation": confirmed obligations outstanding, ending |

I did not use the prior year-end balances or the invoices confirmed and paid during the year. Those were Walmart $5,271, Boeing $2,703 and Pfizer $688.

**No year-end balance found:** NVIDIA, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, Berkshire Hathaway and ExxonMobil. I did not find a supplier finance or supply chain financing disclosure in any of them. I looked at the notes and sections most likely to contain one, such as balance sheet components and payables, but I did not search the full text. Berkshire is the least certain of the five. Treat "no disclosure" as likely rather than confirmed.
